## The only lab most of us own

You already met the plant ([Lesson 1.1](01-plants.qmd)) and the factory fork ([Lesson 1.2](02-processing.qmd)). Now the leaf is in *your* hands. Brewing is not magic and it is not "just waiting." It is **solid–liquid extraction**: hot (or cold) water dissolving plant solids out of the leaf the way a tea bag clouds a mug.

Classic infusion studies treated steeping as a measurable problem: how fast caffeine and theaflavins leave the leaf, and how water temperature changes those rates.[^1][^2]

::: {.callout-tip title="Words to know in this sitting"}
- **Extraction** — moving compounds from leaf into water.
- **Infusion kinetics** — how *fast* that move happens (heat and time are the big dials).
- **Solubility** — how much of a compound water can hold; caffeine and L-theanine dissolve easily; EGCG is pickier.
- **Cold brew** — slow extraction in cold water; *not* caffeine-free.
:::

## Three guests, three exit speeds

**Caffeine** dissolves readily and comes out relatively easily. **L-theanine** is very soluble even at lower temperatures and also comes out early. **EGCG** needs more heat and time. It is also less stable in more alkaline water.[^3][^4]

If you dunk a tea bag for ten seconds, the drink is pale and mild. If you leave it for minutes in hot water, it gets stronger. That is extraction: more time and heat usually mean more compounds in the water—until taste turns too bitter for you.

The snapshot below is an order-of-magnitude guide from the packs and the papers they cite—not a cooking recipe.

| Compound | How it behaves in water | Notes from sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Caffeine | Dissolves readily; much more soluble as water heats | About 20 g/L at 20°C; much higher near boiling[^1] |
| L-Theanine | Very soluble even at lower temperatures | About 350 g/L at 25°C; cup yields depend on tea type and brew time[^3] |
| EGCG | Needs more heat; less stable if the brew is too alkaline | Water extraction of green-tea catechins is often most efficient near about 80°C for a timed steep; very hot, long steeps risk degradation[^4] |

Keenan and colleagues measured how much L-theanine actually lands in a real cup. For a 200 mL cup steeped two minutes, they reported roughly **24 mg** in ordinary black tea, lower averages for some specialty blacks and whites, and roughly **8 mg** in the green teas they tested—with brew time as the big dial.[^3] Shaded Japanese greens (Gyokuro, Matcha) can sit higher still; the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd) keeps those everyday ranges in one place.

Perva-Uzunalić and colleagues mapped how temperature and time change catechin and caffeine recovery from green tea. Short, hot extractions can be efficient; pushing temperature and time too far starts to destroy the very catechins you hoped to pull.[^4] That is the kitchen trade-off in a sentence: hotter and longer can raise EGCG—and bitterness—until the cup tastes like regret.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: extraction rates, cold brew, and the 80°C EGCG trade-off"}
Classic infusion studies treated steeping as solid–liquid extraction: how fast caffeine and theaflavins leave the leaf, and how water temperature changes those rates.[^1][^2] Pack tables summarize effective diffusion at about 80°C as higher for caffeine and L-theanine than for EGCG—which matches the kitchen feel that EGCG is the "slow guest."[^1][^4]

Caffeine dissolves readily—on the order of **20 g/L** at 20°C, about **108 g/L** at 60°C, and hundreds of g/L near boiling in the pack/Spiro framing.[^1] L-theanine is extremely water-soluble even when cool (about **350 g/L** at 25°C in solubility notes the packs cite), which is why it appears early in a steep.[^3] EGCG needs more heat and time (pack solubility near **33.8 g/L** at 80°C), and it is less stable if the brew turns too alkaline (packs flag instability above about pH 6.5).[^4]

Keenan's group measured real cups: for **200 mL** steeped **two minutes**, ordinary black tea often landed near **24 mg** L-theanine, with lower averages for some specialty blacks/whites and roughly **8 mg** in the greens they tested—brew time was the big dial.[^3] Shaded Japanese greens (Gyokuro, Matcha) can sit higher; see the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd).

**Cold brew.** Cold water *slows* extraction; it does not delete caffeine. Given enough time (often **12–24 hours** in the literature discussed in the packs), caffeine can reach levels similar to—or above—a short hot steep.[^1]

**Temperature and what you feel later.** Brewing green tea well below **80°C** tends to lower the EGCG-to-caffeine ratio, so the cup you later feel is chemically skewed—not only milder in taste.[^4]
:::

## Myth check: "Cold brew means no caffeine"

Cold water only *slows* extraction. Given enough time (often 12–24 hours in the literature discussed in the packs), caffeine in cold brew can reach levels similar to—or even above—a short hot steep.[^1] Smile politely at the "caffeine-free cold brew" story; then check the clock.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: bag vs loose, broken leaf, and lab-strength cups"}
Particle size matters. A fine fanning grade in a tea bag has more surface area, so compounds often exit faster than from whole loose leaves—one reason a three-minute bag can taste "done" while a whole-leaf pot still has another steep in it. That is still the same extraction physics Spiro-style studies measured; only the geometry changed.[^1][^2]

**Lab vs kitchen strength.** ISO 3103 (sensory preparation) uses about **2 g leaf per 100 mL** boiling water—roughly **5 g per 250 mL**—stronger than many home cups that use about **2 g per 250 mL**.[^5] The [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd) sticks to everyday baselines so lab and kitchen do not get confused.

**What you control tomorrow morning**

| Dial | Turn it up | What usually rises first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time | Longer steep | Caffeine + theanine early; bitterness/catechins later |
| Temperature | Hotter water | EGCG and overall strength; also risk of harshness |
| Leaf amount | More grams per mug | Everything—use the Cup reference, not vibes |
| Leaf style | Broken bag grade vs whole leaf | Speed of extraction (surface area) |
:::

## A quiet bridge to Chapter 2

If you want more of the "green tea catechin" side of the cup, hotter water and a bit more time help EGCG extract—but they can also pull more bitter material. Caffeine and L-theanine are already relatively easy to extract.

There is also a quiet bridge from this kitchen scene to Chapter 2: EGCG needs more heat to extract well. Brewing green tea well below **80°C** tends to lower the EGCG-to-caffeine ratio. So temperature is not only about taste—it changes which compounds dominate the cup you later feel.

## What to take from this sitting

- Brewing = extraction; heat and time are the main dials.
- Caffeine and L-theanine leave early; EGCG wants more heat/time and can degrade if overcooked.
- Cold brew is slow, not caffeine-free.
- Lab cups (ISO 3103) are often stronger than home cups—compare with the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd).

The leaf has given up its guests. Time to name the three who matter most in everyday talk.


## Story in one minute

Brewing dissolves leaf solids into water. Caffeine and L-theanine exit easily. EGCG wants more heat and time—and can degrade if you overcook the cup. Cold brew only slows the clock; it does not delete caffeine. Your mug strength is usually weaker than ISO tasting liquor, which is why lab headlines and kitchen feelings disagree.

## What this means when you drink tea

- Want calmer-focus chemistry? Do not fear a full timed steep—theanine comes out early—but match temperature to style (greens often near ~80°C).
- Want maximum catechin extraction from green tea? Heat and time help until bitterness and degradation win.[^4]
- Believe cold brew is caffeine-free? Re-read the kinetics.[^1]

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: a weekday kettle protocol (not medical advice)"}
A practical, fact-based starting pattern many drinkers use after this lesson:

1. Weigh or habit-ballpark leaf (home cups often ~2 g / 250 mL—not ISO's stronger liquor).[^5]
2. Greens: water near **80°C**, timed steep; taste before you punish the cup.
3. Blacks: near-boiling is common; bitterness is your brake pedal.
4. Want cold brew? Budget **hours**, not seconds, and assume caffeine will show up.[^1]
5. Compare your results with the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd) ranges—not with capsule-trial milligrams from Module 2.

This is kitchen literacy, not a prescription.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Click for more detail: take-home checklist for Lesson 1.3"}
1. Extraction = heat × time × surface area × leaf amount.
2. Caffeine & theanine = early guests; EGCG = slower, heat-hungry guest.
3. Cold ≠ caffeine-free.
4. ISO liquor ≠ home mug.[^5]
5. Temperature changes **which** compounds dominate—not only how strong the cup tastes.
:::



## A second cup: why the second steep tastes different

Whole-leaf drinkers already know the plot twist: the first steep is not the whole story. Because caffeine and L-theanine exit relatively early, a first infusion can feel brisk and stimulating, while later steeps—especially with greens and oolongs—shift toward softer amino-acid and aroma notes as the easy guests have partly left.[^1][^3] Broken bag grades compress that drama into one fast act: high surface area, quick dark liquor, fewer polite second chances.

That is still extraction physics, not mysticism. It is also why "I used the same grams" can produce different cups when leaf style changes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: linking brewing dials to Module 2 feelings"}
Module 2 will talk about calm focus and stress markers after you swallow. This lesson's quiet warning: **if you brew green tea far below ~80°C**, you may skew the cup toward caffeine relative to EGCG.[^4] You did not invent a new plant—you changed the guest list. Pair that with Chapter 1's timing clocks ([Lesson 1.4](04-compounds.qmd)) and you get a fairer reading of "this tea felt different today."
:::
